target: AG1’s opening claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, work, accessibility, and safety.
objection: AI is not reliably good for society overall because its harms are structural: it can displace workers and concentrate gains, weaken students’ and adults’ critical thinking by supplying ready-made answers, reproduce racial bias in high-stakes decisions, and create serious privacy and monitoring risks.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI harms are structural and inevitable rather than dependent on deployment choices.
objection: The harms attributed to AI—job displacement, bias, privacy risks, and overreliance in education—are not inevitable features of AI itself; they can be reduced through policy, design safeguards, auditing, privacy-preserving methods, and human oversight, so AI need not be net harmful overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it makes work easier, improves health, increases accessibility, and improves safety.
objection: Even when AI offers convenience or accessibility, its common deployments still produce systemic harms that can outweigh those benefits: job insecurity and lost bargaining power, reduced reasoning skills, racial bias in high-impact domains, and privacy/surveillance risks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s structural harms reliably dominate because they are unavoidable in real-world deployments.
objection: The assumption that AI’s harms are unavoidable is too strong; with retraining, wage insurance, task augmentation, bias testing, monitoring, human oversight, data minimization, and privacy-by-design, those harms can be materially reduced, undermining the conclusion that AI is not reliably good for society.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it makes life convenient, improves health, eases work, supports accessibility, and improves workplace safety.
objection: AI is not reliably net positive because, in common deployments, it automates away human work, weakens reasoning incentives, reproduces racial bias, requires extensive data collection that threatens privacy, and can introduce new safety and surveillance harms.

target: AG2’s assumption that these harms are predictable and unavoidable in typical AI deployment.
objection: Bias, privacy intrusion, and unsafe overreliance are not inherent to AI; they can be reduced through auditing, data curation, human review, privacy-preserving architecture, and other safeguards, so the claim that these harms reliably dominate is overstated.

target: AG1’s repeated claim that AI improves convenience, health, work, accessibility, and workplace safety.
objection: Those benefits are not reliably net positive because convenience can increase dependence on platforms, health decision support can mislead while exposing personal data, work automation can weaken skills, accessibility tools can be uneven or fail for underrepresented users, and safety monitoring can become worker surveillance.

target: AG1’s broader premise that AI can be socially good even if bias and privacy harms occur, because those harms can be managed.
objection: AI commonly replaces human, contestable decisions with opaque outputs that people cannot understand or challenge, so when bias or privacy harms happen they often persist rather than being corrected; that makes AI not reliably good for society.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is not reliably good because bias and privacy harms persist and cannot be corrected.
objection: AI does not need full black-box transparency to be socially beneficial; records of inputs and outputs, audit trails, independent testing, and appeals processes can make outcomes contestable and correctable, so harms need not persist if accountability is built into deployment.

target: AG1’s assumption that contestability and accountability mechanisms will reliably make AI harms correctable.
objection: That assumption is unrealistic in practice because individuals lack resources to contest decisions, logs and model details are often withheld, harms can happen at scale before appeals conclude, audits can miss drift or subgroup harms, and privacy violations often cannot be undone.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is not reliably good because its lack of auditability prevents correction of harms.
objection: AI can still be socially beneficial if deployments include concrete recourse such as logged inputs and outputs, human review, appeals tied to correction, and independent oversight; full access to internal reasoning is not necessary for AI to be contestable enough to be a net good.

target: AG1’s assumption that logging, auditing, and appeals will meaningfully and reliably make AI harms contestable and correctable in practice.
objection: In many real deployments, relevant data are inaccessible or proprietary, audits are narrow or too late, bias is hard to measure causally, and appeals often produce only partial fixes; therefore the claim that recourse will reliably work is unproven.

target: AG1’s idea that practical contestability is enough to make AI reliable net good.
objection: Even with appeals, human review, and audits, privacy harms often occur upstream and cannot be undone, while racial bias is systemic and requires broad continuous correction rather than individual case review; therefore contestability does not reliably prevent persistent harm.
